title: WHAT IF YOU GOT A 5-STAR WANTED LEVEL IN REAL LIFE?

segments.line: On Friday, Mo has a plan.
'Three stars. Just to see'.
At the subway station, you hop over the ticket gate.
The third star snaps on.
And then you do what you have learned to do. You run, and you hide.
You crouch behind the dumpsters at the back of the station, and you start counting.
Twenty-eight seconds, your record. Twenty-nine. Thirty. The stars don't even flash.
In the game, this is where you wait it out.
In real life, this is where it stops being a game.
First, the helicopter.
A police helicopter can cruise at about a hundred and fifty miles an hour, faster than anything on the road below.
And it doesn't need to see you. Its thermal camera sees heat.
In 2013, a police helicopter found a man hiding under a cover in a boat, at night, from the heat of his body alone.
Your hiding place behind the dumpsters glows like a light bulb.
Second, the cameras. One company alone has put more than a hundred thousand license plate cameras on American streets.
Every car you get into leaves a trail. And the
city's own cameras, on lampposts and in every station, already have your hoodie, your face, and exactly which way you ran.
Third, the stars don't fade. In real life, a wanted person stays wanted.
In most US states, an arrest warrant has no expiry date.
It doesn't flash and disappear after thirty seconds. It waits. For years.
And here is the part the game never tells you. In every US state, running from the police is a crime of its own.
You jumped a ticket gate, something you could have paid a fine for. Running is what made it serious.
That night, for the first time, you get home, and the three stars are still there.
Mum can't see them. She just asks why there was a helicopter over the subway station all afternoon. You say you don't know.
Ellie says helicopters are cool.
